title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers I: Evaluating Bias in Teacher Value-Added Estimates
research_question: Do predictions of teacher quality based on students' test score gains provide unbiased forecasts of how much a teacher will raise students' achievement, or are such predictions contaminated by the non-random sorting of students to teachers? Specifically, to what extent does student selection on observable and unobservable characteristics bias estimates of individual teachers' contributions to test score gains?
data_description: The analysis uses administrative records from a large urban U.S. school district covering math and English standardized test scores for students in grades 3-8 in elementary and middle schools. The unit of observation is the student-subject-school year, with information on classroom assignments, teachers, lagged test scores, special-education status, and student ethnicity. These school-district records are linked via a multi-step matching algorithm (using date of birth, gender, last name, first name, ZIP code, and place of birth) to U.S. federal income tax records, which provide parental income and other family characteristics. Approximately 88.6% of students and 89.8% of student-subject observations are successfully matched. The estimation sample contains roughly 6.9 million student-subject-year observations, with about 6.1 million having linked parental income data. Teachers' value-added estimates are constructed at the teacher-year level using leave-year-out predictions that allow for drift over time.
institutional_context: Public school districts increasingly use statistical measures of teachers' contributions to student test score gains for high-stakes decisions such as tenure, compensation, and dismissal. A central concern is that students are not randomly assigned to teachers: principals, parents, and scheduling practices may systematically sort students with particular backgrounds, prior achievement, or unobserved characteristics to particular teachers, potentially distorting measures of teacher effectiveness. The setting examined is a large urban U.S. school district where teachers in elementary and middle schools teach math and English, with elementary teachers typically responsible for one classroom per year and middle school teachers teaching multiple classes. Variation in cohort composition and teaching staff arises because teachers enter, leave, or switch grades across years, generating year-to-year changes in the average predicted teacher quality faced by successive cohorts within the same school and grade. This setting allows comparison of test score outcomes across cohorts as the teaching workforce changes.
